Compositional data (CoDa) model of life-table deaths

Source: R/model-coda.R
coda.Rd

coda() is the Lee-Carter model in compositional form (Oeppen 2008) as published by Bergeron-Boucher, Canudas-Romo, Oeppen and Vaupel (2017). It models the life-table distribution of deaths by age, which sums to 1. With coherent = TRUE or common_by, it is their coherent model for several populations (CoDa-coherent). Status: published, with the deviations listed below. Page and equation numbers refer to Bergeron-Boucher et al. (2017).

Usage

coda(
  jump_off = c("observed", "fitted"),
  coherent = FALSE,
  common_by = NULL,
  order = c(0, 1, 1),
  drift = TRUE,
  order_dev = c(1, 1, 0),
  drift_dev = FALSE,
  open = c("auto", "kannisto", "regression")
)

Arguments

jump_off

"observed" (forecasts start from the observed deaths of the last year) or "fitted" (from the fitted deaths).

coherent

Fit the coherent model with a common component per group.

common_by

Stratum variable(s) defining groups with their own common component (implies coherent = TRUE); NULL with coherent = TRUE puts all strata in one group.

order

ARIMA order c(p, d, q) of the index (of the common index in the coherent model); c(0, 1, 1) by default (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017). c(0, 1, 0) with drift = TRUE is the random walk with drift of Lee and Carter (1992), the default of the R package MortalityForecast.

drift

Include a drift (a constant of the differenced index) when d = 1; ignored otherwise (d = 0 includes a mean, d = 2 no constant).

order_dev, drift_dev

ARIMA order and drift of the indexes of the deviations of each stratum in the coherent model; c(1, 1, 0) without drift by default (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017).

open

Treatment of the old ages: "auto" (the Kannisto extension where the age groups allow it, otherwise the regression of the open interval), "kannisto" or "regression".

Value

A model specification.

Details

Model (Section 2.3, Appendix A). For one stratum:

  1. the death rates of each year give life-table deaths d[x, t] with radix 1 at the first age (life_table() conventions);

  2. a[x] is the geometric mean of d[x, t] over the years, closed to 1;

  3. the deaths are centred by perturbation (d[x, t] / a[x], closed) and transformed by the centred log-ratio (clr), eq. (5);

  4. the first component of a singular value decomposition gives clr(d[x, t] / a[x]) = b[x] k[t], eq. (6); b and k sum to zero, and their signs make k increase over the fitting period (p. 533);

  5. k[t] follows an ARIMA(0,1,1) model with drift, fitted by maximum likelihood (order, drift; p. 536 and Appendix A, p. 555, where this order had the best BIC for most of 15 countries);

  6. forecasts are transformed back (inverse clr, perturbation by a, closure, eq. 7) to life-table deaths and then to death rates.

Jump-off (Appendix G, p. 566). With jump_off = "observed" (the default), forecasts are the life-table deaths of the last year T perturbed by the change of the model (eq. 17): d[x, T + j] is proportional to d[x, T] exp(b[x] (k[T + j] - k[T])). With "fitted", forecasts start from the fitted deaths of year T. The point forecast of the ARIMA(0,1,1) index with drift is shifted so that its first step equals the drift (eq. 20), which removes the break that the moving-average term causes in the first forecast year; the package applies the same correction to any ARIMA(0,1,q) index with drift.

Coherent model (Section 2.4, Appendix C). The common component B[x] K[t] is the model above fitted to the average mortality of a group: the arithmetic mean of the death rates of its strata (equal weights, p. 557), turned into life-table deaths. Each stratum i has its own centre a[x, i] and deviation clr(d[x, t, i] / a[x, i] / C[exp(B K)]) = b[x, i] k[t, i] (eq. 8a), the first component of the SVD after removing the common component. K follows the model of order and drift (with eq. 20), each k[t, i] an ARIMA(1,1,0) model without drift (order_dev, drift_dev; p. 537), whose point forecast levels off, so that the point forecasts of the strata do not diverge; their intervals still widen with the horizon. order_dev = c(1, 0, 0) gives an AR(1) process with a mean, which Li and Lee (2005) suggest for their deviations (as cited on p. 531) and whose deviations stay bounded in distribution. Groups are all strata, or each level of common_by; if the data carry a hierarchy (see mt_aggregate_strata()), the average uses the bottom strata only, as li_lee() does.

Draws (Appendix B, pp. 556-557). Draws carry the uncertainty of the estimates and of the index forecasts: the residuals of eq. (5) are resampled cell by cell and added to the fitted component, b and k are estimated again (a is kept, as in the paper), the ARIMA model is fitted again to the new index, and future paths of the index are simulated with innovations resampled from its residuals. ceiling(sqrt(n_draws)) refits share the draws (the paper uses 100 refits with 100 paths each). In the coherent model, the common and the stratum components are simulated independently and added (Appendix B); the draws of the common component are the same for all strata of a group. The draws are then centred on the point forecast: each draw is perturbed by the ratio of the point forecast of the first forecast year to the median of the draws in that year, part by part. This follows the authors' code (CoDaForecast.R, supplementary material of the paper); eq. (19) of the paper shifts the bounds of the intervals of life expectancy so that their median is the point forecast. Draws are expected rates; predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates and the exposures, and no other observation noise. The model weights all parts equally on the clr scale, so the noise of ages with few deaths enters k; its intervals can be wider than those of lee_carter() (p. 543).

Old ages (Appendix C, pp. 557-558). With single-year age groups from 80 (at least to 89) and open = "auto" (the default) or "kannisto", the rates from age 80 are replaced in every year by a Kannisto model (Thatcher, Kannisto and Vaupel 1998) fitted by Poisson maximum likelihood to the deaths and exposures of the single ages 80 to 100 of the grid (the authors' code fits ages 80-100 of the Human Mortality Database, open interval 110+) and applied up to age 120, where the life table closes; the single ages 80-120 are parts of the composition. The rate of an open age interval is the forecast deaths over the forecast person-years of its parts, and the forecasts of the ages from 80 are those of the smoothed rates. Other age groups (for example 5-year groups) do not allow this extension. Then, with open = "auto" or "regression", the deaths of an open interval are the survivors at its lower bound, and its log death rate gets loadings on the same indexes, estimated by least squares: log m[open, t] = a_o + b_o k[t] (coherent model: a_o[i] + B_o K[t] + b_o[i] k[t, i], B_o from the log of the average rate of the group); a closed age range adds the survivors at its upper bound as a part. Both are package-specific (reference unknown).

Zero deaths (Appendix C, p. 558). Zero counts of the ages that keep their own rates (below 80 with the Kannisto extension, all ages otherwise) are replaced multiplicatively in each year: each zero gets the share delta of the deaths of the year, the other shares are multiplied by 1 - z delta (z zeros), and delta is half the smallest positive count over all ages and years divided by the deaths of the year. A warning is given when more than 10% of the cells are zero. Package safeguards: the imputed share of a year is at most 1/2, and a year whose deaths at ages from 80 allow no Kannisto fit takes the fit to all years together (with a warning).

Deviations from the paper. Besides the package-specific treatment of other age groups: the life tables use a_x = n / 2 at every age (the authors' code uses 0.06 at age 0); the residuals of the bootstrap are those of eq. (5), as the paper describes (the authors' code takes them around the in-sample one-step forecasts of the ARIMA model); the number of refits follows n_draws; the draws are centred as in the authors' code (see above).

References

Oeppen J (2008). Coherent forecasting of multiple-decrement life tables: a test using Japanese cause of death data. CODAWORK'08, Universitat de Girona. https://hdl.handle.net/10256/742

Bergeron-Boucher M-P, Canudas-Romo V, Oeppen J, Vaupel JW (2017). Coherent forecasts of mortality with compositional data analysis. Demographic Research 37(17): 527-566. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2017.37.17

Thatcher AR, Kannisto V, Vaupel JW (1998). The Force of Mortality at Ages 80 to 120. Odense University Press.

Li N, Lee R (2005). Coherent mortality forecasts for a group of populations: an extension of the Lee-Carter method. Demography 42(3): 575-594. doi:10.1353/dem.2005.0021

Lee RD, Carter LR (1992). Modeling and forecasting U.S. mortality. Journal of the American Statistical Association 87(419): 659-671.

See also

coda_causes() for causes of death, lee_carter() for the model of death rates, li_lee() for its coherent version.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2012)
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(coda(), x), h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
fc2 <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(coda(coherent = TRUE), x), h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
# random walk with drift for the index (Lee and Carter 1992)
fc3 <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(coda(order = c(0, 1, 0)), x), h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
